name: Apalai
catalog_quote: Do ponto de vista fonológico, a palavra é uma seqüência de sílabas em que a penúltima é acentuada: paruru 'banana'. Há um pequeno número de palavras com uma só sílaba. Estas podem receber o acento intensivo dependendo de sua posição em construções maiores

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding Portuguese sentence and the secondary-stress/non-contrastive sentences are verbatim in the held SIL re-edition ( p. 5) and, after fetching the original 1971 scan from the Curt Nimuendajú library, confirmed at printed p. 26 exactly as the locator says. (2) Deciding source: a 1971 primary phonology article by the language's principal describers (Koehn & Koehn, SIL), not a database paraphrase; StressTyp2/Gordon 2002 are listed only as secondary refs. Best available: the only fuller work is the same authors' 1986 HAL sketch (not held, paywalled); Derbyshire 1999:28 (held elsewhere in the catalog tree) independently gives Apalai penultimate stress; Gomes & Ferreira 2020 (fetched sources) document that no later phonological/prosodic study of Apalaí exists, and web searches (SIL archive, Brazilian repositories, JIPA/phonology journals) found none.

sources.quote: "From the phonological point of view, the word is a sequence of syllables in which the penultimate is stressed: parúru 'banana'." And: "Secondary stress falls on closed syllables and on nasal syllables adjacent to at least one unstressed syllable... Secondary stress may fall on the initial syllable of words of four or more syllables when the second syllable is not stressed: xìrikazúru 'grass'. ... The stress patterns, however, are never contrastive."

sources.quote: 'Many languages have weight-sensitive rhythmic (iambic) stress (Table 1; Meira, 1998); some, however, have simple cumulative, usually penultimate, stress (Panare, Bakairi, Kuikuro, Yukpa).' Apalai is not named in either group.

sources.note: The reference-grammar sketch by the same fieldworkers, 15 years after the 12-page 1971 phonemic statement our coding rests on; its suprasegmentals subsection is the fullest published statement of Apalai stress and would settle whether the 'flexibility' and closed-syllable secondary stresses of 1971 were later reanalysed (e.g. as weight-sensitivity). Derbyshire 1999:28 (held) already summarises AP as penultimate, so a change of primary-stress coding is unlikely.
